security_spec.violation_condition: Linux kernel code in KVM or trap emulation paths inspects csr[9:8] to determine CSR privilege level for access-control decisions, but fails to recognize the encoding 0b10 as hypervisor-level, thereby misclassifying hypervisor CSRs (0x600-0x6ff range, e.g. hstatus, hedeleg, hgatp) as belonging to user (0b00) or supervisor (0b01) privilege and allowing reads/writes at an insufficient privilege level.
security_spec.summary: Any kernel CSR access-control or emulation path that decodes csr[9:8] for privilege gating must know that 0b10 maps to 'hypervisor'; misinterpreting it as user or supervisor allows guest-controlled CSR read/write from VS-mode that should be blocked.

findings.finding: CSR number extracted via 'csr_num = insn >> SH_RS2' (line 150), which gets the full 12-bit CSR address from instruction bits [31:20]. No csr[9:8] privilege-bit inspection exists. Access control relies on hardware enforcement (CPU traps illegal-privilege CSR accesses as EXC_VIRTUAL_INST_FAULT or EXC_INST_ILLEGAL). The csr_funcs[] lookup table (line 112-116) uses exact 12-bit CSR numbers (e.g., CSR_SIREG=0x151, CSR_CYCLE=0xc00, CSR_SEED=0x015) with no partial bitfield matching. Unknown CSRs (including all hypervisor 0x600 range) fall through to userspace QEMU emulation (line 221-224).

The 12-bit CSR number (csr_num) extracted at line 150 is used without any validation of the implicit privilege field in bits [9:8]. The kernel forwards unknown CSRs directly to userspace (QEMU) via KVM_EXIT_RISCV_CSR at line 223. If a hardware erratum or nested-virtualization scenario caused a hypervisor-only CSR (e.g., HSTATUS=0x600, HEDELEG=0x602, HGATP=0x680) to reach this handler when the guest is at an insufficient privilege level, the kernel would blindly forward it to userspace without detecting the privilege mismatch. Currently mitigated by hardware correctly enforcing CSR privilege and csr_funcs[] not containing any 0x600-range entries.

Dispatcher for SYSTEM opcode instructions. Only matches on instruction opcode masks (CSRRW, CSRRS, CSRRC, etc.) — privilege-agnostic. Correctly delegates KVM_INSN_ILLEGAL_TRAP to truly_illegal_insn() which redirects as EXC_INST_ILLEGAL to guest, preserving hardware-level privilege enforcement.

EXC_VIRTUAL_INST_FAULT entry point checks HSTATUS_SPV to confirm trap was taken from VS-mode before dispatching to kvm_riscv_vcpu_virtual_insn(). No CSR privilege bit inspection — hardware has already determined the CSR access was illegal for the guest's privilege mode.

Host kernel illegal-instruction trap handler. Does NOT decode the CSR number at all. On illegal instruction (including illegal CSR access), attempts riscv_v_first_use_handler() for vector extension lazy-init, then sends SIGILL. No CSR privilege-level checking code exists here. Hardware enforcement is the sole access control mechanism.

Handles CSR_SIREG (0x151, bits[9:8]=01, Supervisor) and CSR_STOPEI (0x15c, bits[9:8]=01, Supervisor) emulation. These are correctly supervisor-level CSRs. No hypervisor CSR range (0x200 or 0x600) is handled. The function ignores the csr_num parameter — it reads VSISELECT instead to determine which indirect register to access. No privilege-bit decoding anywhere.

CSR address definitions show correct privilege-level mapping per the RISC-V spec. VS-level CSRs (0x200-0x2FF) have bits[9:8]=10 (hypervisor). HS-level CSRs (0x600-0x6FF: HSTATUS, HEDELEG, HGATP etc.) also have bits[9:8] that would decode as 00 in the low 10 bits, but with bits[11:10]=01 distinguishing them from user CSRs. No code in the kernel inspects only bits[9:8] for privilege determination — all lookups use the full 12-bit address.
